stories.title: The Boy with the Blue Notebook

pages.text: Faris had been waiting all season for the final of the Jeddah Schools Cup. Then, two weeks before the big match, he twisted his ankle during training and heard the doctor say the words he feared most: "Six weeks of rest." That evening he sat on the balcony with his leg on a cushion, watching the boys in the street play under the streetlights. He felt as if someone had locked him out of his own life.

The next day, Coach Hamdan visited his house with a small blue notebook. "You can't run, Faris, but you can still see," he said. "Al-Noor Academy are our opponents in the final, and I want you to watch every video of their matches. Write down anything strange you notice, even if it seems small." Faris wasn't sure, but he opened his laptop that night and pressed play.

At first he only saw what everyone saw: fast wingers, a tall defender, and a captain named Saad who never seemed to get tired. But after the fourth video, Faris began to notice patterns. Al-Noor's goalkeeper always came out too early on corners, and Saad touched his sleeve every time he was about to take a penalty. Faris paused, rewound, and watched again. Each time Saad touched his left sleeve, the ball went to the right, and when he touched his right sleeve, it went left.

He showed his notes to Yousef, the team's goalkeeper, at the next training session, but Yousef just laughed. "You've been watching too much TV, my friend. Penalties are about luck, not sleeves." Faris felt his face go hot, but he didn't give up. "Just remember it," he said quietly, "because if it isn't true, you've lost nothing."

The final was played on a warm Thursday evening, and the stands were packed with families waving green and white flags. Faris sat on the bench beside the coach, with his crutches lying on the grass. Al-Noor scored first, but Faris's team equalised just before half-time when their striker headed in a corner. The goalkeeper had come out too early, exactly as the notebook had predicted, and after ninety minutes the score was still 1-1.

The penalty shootout was tense. Both teams scored their first four penalties, and the crowd fell almost silent. Then Saad walked forward to take Al-Noor's last kick. Faris held his breath as the captain placed the ball, stepped back and, without thinking, touched his left sleeve.

Yousef glanced towards the bench, and Faris gave the smallest nod. Saad ran up and struck the ball hard and low to the right, but Yousef was already diving. His fingertips pushed the ball around the post, and the stadium exploded with noise. A moment later their own captain scored, and the cup was theirs.

In the celebrations, Yousef ran straight past his teammates to the bench and lifted Faris off the ground, crutches and all. "Sleeves!" he shouted. "I'll never laugh at your notebook again!" Later, Saad came over, shook Faris's hand and joked, "Next season I'll have to keep my hands in my pockets." Faris laughed, and for the first time in weeks, his ankle didn't seem to matter at all.

questions.q: Why couldn't Faris play in the final?
options: He had twisted his ankle in training.
The coach chose another player.
He was travelling with his family.

questions.q: What did Faris notice about Saad's penalties?
options: He always kicked the ball to the left.
He touched one sleeve and kicked to the opposite side.
He looked at the goalkeeper before every kick.

questions.q: In the story, the word "equalised" means:
options: lost the match
made the score the same
stopped the game

questions.q: How did Yousef feel about Faris's notes at first?
options: He thought they were silly and laughed.
He was very excited about them.
He was angry that Faris had written them.

questions.q: What is the main lesson of the story?
options: Penalties are only about luck.
Goalkeepers are the most important players.
You can still help your team in different ways, even when you can't play.

stories.title: The Night Visitor of the Old Bookshop

pages.text: Every summer, Faisal stayed with his grandfather in the old part of Jeddah, where the houses had tall wooden windows called roshans. His grandfather owned a small bookshop on the ground floor of one of these houses. One morning, Faisal found Grandfather standing in the middle of the shop, looking confused. "Someone has been here during the night," he said quietly. "But the door was locked, and nothing is missing."

Faisal looked around the shop. Six books were lying on the reading table, although Grandfather was sure he had put every book back on the shelves before closing. No money was missing from the drawer, and the old lock on the door hadn't been damaged. "Maybe you just forgot," Faisal suggested, but his grandfather shook his head. "I have closed this shop the same way for forty years," he replied.

That afternoon, Faisal's sister Lama arrived from Riyadh, and he told her everything. Lama loved puzzles, so she immediately asked to see the six books. She turned them over one by one, and suddenly she smiled. "Look at the titles," she said. "Every single book is about the stars and planets, so our visitor isn't a thief. He's someone who wants to learn."

The next night, the two of them hid Faisal's phone on a high shelf and left it recording. Before going upstairs, Lama examined the roshan above the reading table. One of its wooden panels was slightly loose, and caught on its edge was a short piece of blue thread. "Whoever comes in is small enough to climb through here," she whispered. "And he's wearing something blue."

In the morning, they rushed downstairs and played the video. At first there was only darkness, but just after midnight the loose panel opened and a thin boy climbed carefully into the shop. He switched on a small torch, took a book about the moon from the shelf and sat reading for nearly two hours. Before he left, he did something unexpected: he wiped the table clean with his sleeve.

Grandfather leaned closer to the screen and sighed. "That's Yousef, the son of the man who repairs shoes at the end of the street," he said. "His family has had a difficult year." Later that day, Faisal saw Yousef in the market and noticed a small tear in the sleeve of his blue jacket. Instead of calling out to him, Faisal decided they should talk to him gently, without embarrassing him.

That evening, Grandfather invited Yousef in for tea. At first the boy stared at the floor with a red face, but finally he admitted everything. "I'm sorry," he said. "I wanted to study astronomy, but I couldn't afford the books, and I was too ashamed to ask." Grandfather was silent for a moment, and Faisal wondered whether he was angry.

Then the old man reached into his pocket and placed a shiny key on the table. "Climbing through windows is dangerous," he said with a smile. "From tomorrow, you will help me in the shop after school, and you can borrow any book you like." That night, on the roof under a sky full of stars, Yousef proudly showed Faisal and Lama the planet Jupiter, and the mystery of the bookshop ended with a new friendship.

questions.q: Why was Grandfather sure that someone had been in the shop?
options: Six books were on the reading table although he had put them all away.
Money was missing from the drawer.
The lock on the door was broken.

questions.q: What clue helped Lama understand that the visitor was not a thief?
options: The visitor left a letter.
All the books were about stars and planets.
The visitor paid for the books.

questions.q: In the story, the word "loose" (page 4) means:
options: very old and dirty
not firmly fixed in its place
painted a different colour

questions.q: Why did Faisal decide not to call out to Yousef in the market?
options: He was afraid of Yousef.
He wanted to call the police first.
He didn't want to embarrass him in front of people.

questions.q: What can we infer about Grandfather from the ending?
options: He is kind and wants to help Yousef learn.
He wants Yousef to pay for the books.
He plans to sell his bookshop.

stories.title: The Boy Who Read the Sky

pages.text: Talal had loved the stars for as long as he could remember. While other boys in his class talked about football, he filled a notebook with careful drawings of constellations and their names. His best friend, Majed, was the only person who knew about the notebook. At least, that was true until last Thursday.

During the school break, Majed had grabbed the notebook and read it aloud as a joke. "Look, everyone! Talal is going to be the first Saudi on the moon!" he shouted, and the whole class burst out laughing. Talal said nothing, but his face burned with shame. Since that day, he hadn't spoken a single word to Majed.

Unfortunately, their families had planned a weekend camping trip near AlUla months before, because their fathers were old friends. In the car, Majed kept trying to start a conversation, but Talal stared out of the window at the orange rocks. "Are you still angry with me?" Majed finally asked. "I trusted you," Talal answered quietly, and that was all he said.

That evening, the adults were making tea by the fire while the younger children played among the rocks. Suddenly, Majed's mother stood up. "Where is Bader?" she called, her voice full of fear. Majed's seven-year-old brother had disappeared into the darkness. The fathers took their torches and hurried off in different directions, telling the two older boys to stay at the camp.

But Majed couldn't just sit and wait. "Bader kept talking about the huge rock that looks like an elephant," he said. "I'm sure he went there." Talal hesitated for a moment, then picked up his own torch. "I'm coming with you," he said, and they found the little boy sitting behind the rock, crying and too frightened to move.

Getting back, however, was much harder than they had expected. Every sand hill looked the same, their phones had no signal, and they could no longer see the glow of the fire. "We're lost," Majed said, starting to panic. Talal looked up at the sky and pointed. "That bright one is the North Star, and our camp was south of the rock, so if we keep the star behind us, we'll be walking in the right direction."

They walked slowly, with Talal checking the sky every few minutes and Majed holding his brother's hand tightly. After about twenty minutes, they saw an orange light shining between the hills. Their mothers ran towards them, and the fathers, who had just returned, looked extremely relieved. "How on earth did you find your way back?" Majed's father asked. "Talal did it," Majed replied. "He read the sky like a map."

Later, by the fire, Majed handed Talal a small glass of tea. "I'm sorry," he said. "I made fun of the very thing that saved us tonight, and I really let you down." Talal smiled for the first time in a week. "Next Thursday, you can tell the class what happened," he said, and Majed laughed. "Deal, and I'll tell them that the first Saudi on the moon is my best friend."

questions.q: Why did Talal stop speaking to Majed?
options: Majed read Talal's star notebook aloud and made the class laugh at him.
Majed lost Talal's notebook at school.
Majed refused to go on the camping trip.

questions.q: Where did the boys find Bader?
options: Next to the car
Behind the rock that looks like an elephant
Near the fire with the adults

questions.q: In the story, the word "relieved" means:
options: very angry
happy because a worry has ended
tired after walking

questions.q: How did Talal know which way to walk back to the camp?
options: He used the map on his phone.
He followed the footprints in the sand.
He used the North Star to find the direction.

questions.q: What can we understand from the ending of the story?
options: Majed now respects Talal's hobby, and their friendship is stronger.
Talal has decided to stop studying the stars.
The two boys will never go camping together again.

stories.title: The Stone That Fell on Hail

pages.text: It was nearly midnight when a bright green light raced across the sky above Hail. Lina, who was on the roof with her older brother Omar, almost dropped her telescope. "Did you see that?" she whispered. The light broke into pieces, and a few seconds later they heard a deep sound, like distant thunder.

The next morning, the family group chat was full of videos. People from three different towns had filmed the fireball. "If it was a meteor, some pieces might have reached the ground," Omar said as he watched the clips again. Lina's eyes lit up. "Each video shows the light from a different direction. If we draw those directions on a map, the lines should meet!"

They spent the afternoon at the kitchen table with a large map, a ruler and a lot of patience. By using the mountains in the background of each video, they worked out which way every camera had been pointing. Slowly, three pencil lines crossed at one point in the desert, about forty kilometres north of their home. Their father looked over their shoulders. "That isn't a guess anymore," he said, impressed. "That's science."

On Friday, after prayers, their father drove them out in his old jeep with water, hats and a strong magnet tied to a stick. "Most meteorites contain iron," Lina explained, "so the magnet will help us tell them apart from ordinary rocks." For two hours they walked in straight lines across the hot sand, but every dark stone they picked up was just volcanic rock. Omar was beginning to lose hope.

Then Lina noticed something strange: a small hole in the sand, with darker sand thrown around it as if something had landed hard. She knelt down and moved the magnet closer. With a sharp click, a black stone the size of a date jumped out of the sand and stuck to it. Its surface was smooth and shiny, as though it had once been melted.

"That's the fusion crust," Omar said, his voice shaking with excitement. "It forms when a meteorite burns as it falls through the atmosphere." Lina turned the stone over in her hands; it was much heavier than it looked. "It has travelled millions of kilometres to get here," she said quietly. "It might even be older than the Earth itself."

That evening, they had to make a difficult decision. A man online had already offered a lot of money for any piece of the meteorite. However, their father reminded them that scientists could learn about the early solar system from it. After a long discussion, they agreed to contact the Saudi Geological Survey, and two experts soon arrived to examine their find.

Weeks later, a letter arrived with wonderful news. The stone had been confirmed as a rare type of meteorite, and it had been given an official name: "Hail North." Today it sits in a museum case, with a small card beside it that shows Lina and Omar's names. Lina still climbs onto the roof at night, but now she doesn't just watch the sky — she asks it questions.

questions.q: How did Lina and Omar find the place where the meteorite probably landed?
options: They drew lines on a map using videos from three towns
They followed the smoke in the desert
A scientist told them where to look

questions.q: Why did they take a magnet into the desert?
options: To find their way home
Because most meteorites contain iron
To keep the jeep safe

questions.q: In the story, the word "ordinary" is closest in meaning to:
options: rare
normal
heavy

questions.q: What is the "fusion crust"?
options: A hole the meteorite makes in the sand
The smooth surface formed when a meteorite burns in the atmosphere
A type of volcanic rock

questions.q: What can we infer about the family from their decision at the end?
options: They valued science and knowledge more than money
They were afraid of the man online
They did not believe the stone was real

pages.text: Lina had always imagined the desert as a silent place. But on her first night at Uncle Khalid's research camp in the Empty Quarter, she heard something strange: a deep, low hum, like a plane flying far away. "That's a dune singing," her cousin Omar said, grinning at her surprised face. "Dad has spent three years trying to understand it."

The next morning, over a breakfast of dates and warm bread, Uncle Khalid explained. "When dry sand slides down a steep dune, the grains rub together and make a booming sound," he said. "We've put microphones across the dunes for kilometres in every direction, so we can record every song they sing." He pointed proudly at a computer screen covered in coloured lines. "These microphones can even tell us exactly where a sound is coming from."

After lunch, the team's drone stopped sending pictures and disappeared somewhere behind the dunes. "It can't be far," Omar said. "We'll take the small buggy and be back before the sun gets low." Uncle Khalid agreed, but he made them promise to take water and a radio, and to stay on the track.

They found the drone easily, lying on its side next to a dry bush. However, as Omar was putting it in the back of the buggy, the sky in the west turned a strange orange-brown colour. "Sandstorm," he whispered. Within minutes, the wind was throwing sand at their faces, and they could hardly see their own hands.

They covered their faces with scarves and sat close to the buggy until the storm had passed. When the air finally cleared, everything looked different, because the track had vanished under fresh sand. Worse, the radio had been damaged by the flying sand. "Hello? Can anyone hear me?" Omar tried again and again, but there was only a crackling noise.

Lina looked around, feeling her heart beating fast. Then she noticed a huge dune nearby, its smooth side shining gold in the late afternoon sun. "Omar, do you remember what your dad said? The microphones can tell where a sound is coming from!" Omar stared at her for a second, and then his face lit up.

It took them twenty minutes to climb to the top, as their feet sank deeper with every step. Together they sat on the edge and pushed themselves forward, sliding down the steep side while sand poured around them. Suddenly the whole dune began to roar, so loudly that Lina could feel it in her chest. They climbed up and slid down three more times, until their arms and legs ached.

An hour later, they saw headlights coming over the sand. Uncle Khalid jumped out of the car and hugged them both tightly. "Our computer said a dune was singing in the wrong place at the wrong time," he laughed. "I knew it had to be you!" That night, Lina lay awake listening, and the desert no longer felt silent at all. It felt like a friend who had answered when they called.

questions.q: What makes a dune 'sing', according to Uncle Khalid?
options: Dry sand grains rubbing together as they slide down
Strong wind blowing through dry bushes
Planes flying low over the desert

questions.q: Why did Lina and Omar go out in the buggy?
options: To find a lost camel
To look for the team's missing drone
To check the microphones after the storm

questions.q: In the story, the track 'vanished' under fresh sand. What does 'vanished' mean?
options: Became wider
Disappeared
Turned orange

questions.q: Why couldn't Omar call the camp for help?
options: He had left the radio at the camp
The radio had been damaged in the sandstorm
The camp was too far away for the radio

questions.q: Why did Uncle Khalid guess that the children were near the singing dune?
options: He saw them climbing it through his binoculars
The drone sent him a picture of them
The dune made a sound at an unusual time and place, so someone must have made it sing

stories.title: The Parrot Who Stole the Speech

pages.text: When Faisal's English teacher chose him to give a speech at the school's English Day, he felt proud and terrified at the same time. His topic was 'Why We Must Save Water', and he had exactly one week to prepare. Every evening he locked himself in his room and practised out loud. His only listener was Captain, his grandmother's grey parrot, who lived in a large cage by the window.

Captain was an excellent audience. He never yawned, and he always listened with his head on one side, as if he were a serious judge. 'Every drop counts!' Faisal would shout at the end of each speech, and Captain would flap his wings. By the end of the week, Faisal knew the speech perfectly. Unfortunately, so did Captain.

On Friday, the whole family came to Grandma's house for lunch. Uncle Hamad went to wash his hands and, as usual, he left the tap running while he talked about football. Suddenly a loud voice came from the cage: 'Every drop counts! Turn it off!' Everyone burst out laughing, and Uncle Hamad turned as red as a tomato.

After that, Captain seemed to think he was in charge of the house. When Aunt Noura poured more tea than anyone could drink, he cried, 'We are wasting our future!' When cousin Majed reached for his third piece of kunafa, Captain screamed, 'Think before you take!' Grandma laughed so hard that she had to wipe the tears from her eyes.

On Monday morning, Faisal stood on the stage in front of hundreds of students and teachers. He had butterflies in his stomach, and when he opened his mouth, his mind went completely blank. Not a single word came out. Then, in the silence, he suddenly heard Captain's squeaky voice in his head: 'Every drop counts!' To his own surprise, he smiled.

'I have to be honest with you,' Faisal told the audience. 'I practised this speech in front of a parrot, and now he gives it much better than I do.' The hall exploded with laughter, and somehow his fear disappeared. He gave the whole speech confidently, and at the end he copied Captain's voice exactly: 'Every drop counts! Turn it off!' The students cheered so loudly that the head teacher had to raise his hand for quiet.

Faisal did not win first place, because his classmate Omar had given a brilliant speech full of facts and numbers. However, the head teacher announced a special Audience Prize, which the students had voted for. 'This is the speech that everyone will remember,' he said, handing Faisal a shiny trophy. Faisal could hardly believe it.

That evening, Faisal placed the trophy next to Captain's cage. 'Half of this belongs to you,' he said, and the parrot proudly puffed out his feathers. Just then, they heard water running in the bathroom, and Captain opened his beak. But before he could say a word, Uncle Hamad rushed to turn off the tap. 'I am not going to be told off by a parrot twice!' he said, and the whole family laughed until their sides hurt.

options: Why we must save water
How to look after parrots
Why football is important

questions.q: Why did Uncle Hamad turn red at lunch?
options: He ate too much kunafa
The parrot told him to turn off the tap
He forgot to bring a present

questions.q: In the story, 'his mind went completely blank' means that Faisal...
options: felt very sleepy
suddenly forgot what he wanted to say
started thinking about many things

questions.q: What helped Faisal to stop feeling afraid on the stage?
options: The head teacher gave him his notes
Omar whispered the words to him
He remembered Captain and made the audience laugh

questions.q: What can we guess about Uncle Hamad at the end of the story?
options: He has learned to be more careful with water
He wants to buy his own parrot
He is angry with Faisal for winning

pages.text: Every winter, Faris spent a week with his uncle Khalid on the Farasan Islands, far out in the Red Sea. His uncle was a marine biologist who studied sea turtles, and Faris thought it was the best job in the world. This year, however, Uncle Khalid looked worried when he met him at the ferry. "Do you remember Noura?" he asked.

Of course Faris remembered. Noura was a green turtle that they had rescued together two years earlier, and before releasing her, his uncle had attached a small satellite tracker to her shell. Since then, Faris had checked her journey on his phone almost every night. "Her signal hasn't moved for three days," Uncle Khalid explained. "Either the tracker is broken, or she's in trouble."

Early the next morning, they set off in the research boat with Captain Saeed, an old fisherman who knew these waters better than anyone. The sea was calm and as smooth as glass, and dolphins raced alongside the boat for a while. But Faris couldn't enjoy the view. He kept staring at the small dot on the screen, which still hadn't moved at all.

When they reached the location, Captain Saeed slowed the engine and frowned. "Ghost net," he said quietly, pointing at something dark floating just under the surface. Faris had read about ghost nets: old fishing nets that are lost or thrown away and continue to catch animals for years. Then he saw a flipper moving weakly inside the tangle.

Uncle Khalid put on his mask and fins and slipped into the water, and Faris, who had passed a snorkelling course last summer, was allowed to follow him. Underwater, the net looked even worse, wrapped around the coral and full of plastic bottles. Noura was caught tightly, and she was struggling to reach the surface to breathe. Faris held the net steady while his uncle cut it carefully with a special knife.

It seemed to take forever, although it was probably only a few minutes. At last, the final piece of rope came loose, and Noura shot upwards like a rocket. She took a long, deep breath at the surface, and Faris wanted to cheer through his snorkel. They had arrived in the nick of time.

Back on the boat, the three of them pulled the heavy net out of the sea so that it could never trap another animal. "My father used to say that the sea gives us everything, so we must look after it," Captain Saeed said, wiping his hands. Uncle Khalid nodded and checked the tracker. The dot was moving again, heading south toward the open sea.

That night, Faris sat on the beach with his phone, watching Noura's dot travel further and further away. He had come to the islands expecting a relaxing holiday, but he was going home with a new plan. "When I grow up, I'm going to do your job," he told his uncle. Uncle Khalid smiled. "You already did it today," he replied.

questions.q: Why was Uncle Khalid worried at the start of the story?
options: Noura's signal had not moved for three days.
The research boat was broken.
Faris had missed the ferry.

questions.q: What is a 'ghost net'?
options: A net used by scientists to catch turtles
An old, lost fishing net that keeps catching animals
A net that is impossible to see in the dark

questions.q: Why was Faris allowed to go into the water with his uncle?
options: Captain Saeed asked him to.
He had passed a snorkelling course.
Noura knew him and would not be afraid.

questions.q: In the story, 'in the nick of time' means:
options: just before it was too late
much too early
after a very long journey

questions.q: What does Uncle Khalid mean when he says, "You already did it today"?
options: Faris has already finished his holiday.
Faris worked like a real turtle scientist by helping to save Noura.
Faris has already got a job on the islands.

pages.text: Every summer, Yusuf spent his holidays on his grandfather's date farm in Al-Ahsa. Grandfather Saleh had looked after the palms for fifty years, and he could tell when a tree needed water just by touching its leaves. "A good farmer listens to his trees," he always said. Yusuf, who was thirteen and loved electronics, had a different idea: what if the trees could actually speak?

For three weeks, Yusuf worked on his invention in a corner of the farm storeroom. He used a small sensor that measured how wet the soil was, a cheap computer board and parts from his old broken phone. His older sister Maha, who was studying computer science, helped him write the code. When the soil became too dry, the device would send a message to Grandfather's phone: "I'm thirsty!"

Grandfather laughed when he saw the box of wires pushed into the sand beside a young palm. "My phone already gets enough messages from your aunts," he joked. "I don't need messages from trees as well." Yusuf smiled, but he felt a little hurt. He had already entered his invention in the regional young inventors' competition, and he was determined to prove that it worked.

On the day of the competition, the hall was full of clever ideas, from a robot that sorted rubbish to a lamp powered by a bicycle. Yusuf set up his display nervously and waited for the judges. But when he pressed the button to show them how it worked, nothing happened. The battery was dead, because he had forgotten to charge it the night before. The judges nodded politely, wrote something down and moved on, and Yusuf went home without a prize.

"Back to the drawing board," Maha said kindly in the car, but Yusuf didn't reply. That night he couldn't sleep, so he lay on the roof of the farmhouse, looking at the stars. He thought about giving up and throwing the whole thing away. Then, at two o'clock in the morning, Grandfather's phone buzzed loudly downstairs.

Grandfather came out with sleepy eyes, holding the phone. "Your tree says it's thirsty," he said in surprise. "But I watered all the young palms this evening." They hurried outside with a torch and discovered that the old pump had stopped working, and the water channels were completely dry.

"If we had waited until morning, the young palms wouldn't have survived tomorrow's heat," Grandfather said quietly. Together, they worked until sunrise, fixing the pump and clearing the channels so the water could flow again. Yusuf's hands were covered in mud, but he had never felt happier. As the sun came up, Grandfather put his arm around his grandson's shoulders.

The following week, Grandfather surprised everyone by asking for twenty more devices, one for every row of palms. "I still listen to my trees," he told his friends proudly, "but now my grandson has taught them how to call me." Yusuf didn't win a prize that year, but he learned something more valuable: an invention isn't finished until it solves a real problem. Next year, he would enter the competition again, and this time he would remember to charge the battery!

questions.q: How did Grandfather Saleh usually know when a palm needed water?
options: He touched its leaves.
He checked a message on his phone.
He measured the soil with a machine.

questions.q: Why did Yusuf's invention not work at the competition?
options: The judges pressed the wrong button.
He had forgotten to charge the battery.
The sensor was broken by the sand.

questions.q: Maha says "Back to the drawing board." What does she mean?
options: Yusuf should start drawing pictures instead.
It's time to stop working on the invention forever.
Yusuf needs to try again and improve his idea.

questions.q: Why were the channels dry even though Grandfather had watered the palms that evening?
options: The old pump had stopped working.
Yusuf had turned off the water.
The heat had dried them in one hour.

questions.q: What can we understand about Grandfather at the end of the story?
options: He still thinks the invention is a silly toy.
He now respects Yusuf's invention and combines it with his old knowledge.
He has decided to stop farming and sell the palms.

pages.text: Sami had been looking forward to the family trip to Abha for weeks. When the plane landed, he could already see green mountains and thick white clouds through the window. At the baggage belt, he quickly grabbed a blue suitcase with a yellow ribbon on the handle. His mother always tied a ribbon on their bags so they would never lose them.

At the hotel, Sami opened the suitcase to find his football shirt. Instead, he found paintbrushes, small tubes of paint and a thick sketchbook. "This isn't mine!" he shouted. His father looked closely at the ribbon and laughed. "Someone else had the same idea as your mother, it seems."

The airline office at the airport was closed until the next morning, and there was no name tag on the suitcase. Sami sat on his bed and turned the pages of the sketchbook carefully. There were drawings of the airport, a plane wing and a sleeping passenger. The last page showed an unfinished picture of tall stone houses with colourful windows. "That's Rijal Almaa," said his father. "It's a famous old village near here."

"Maybe the artist is going there to finish this painting," Sami said excitedly. "We could find him and return his things!" His father shook his head. "Finding one man in a village full of tourists would be like looking for a needle in a haystack." But his mother smiled. "We were planning to visit Rijal Almaa anyway, weren't we?"

Early the next day, they drove down narrow mountain roads while fog floated around the car. When they arrived, the village looked exactly like the drawing, but much more amazing. Sami walked slowly between the old houses, studying every visitor who was holding a camera or a notebook. After an hour, he was beginning to lose hope.

Then he noticed an elderly man sitting on a low wall, drawing with nothing but a pencil. The man kept sighing and looking at the colourful windows as if they were making him sad. Sami took a deep breath and walked over. "Excuse me, sir," he said politely. "Are you missing some paints, by any chance?"

The man stared at him, then burst out laughing. "You must be the boy with my suitcase!" he said. "I'm Mr. Hassan. Your bag is safe at my hotel, and I've already called the airline about it." He explained that he had travelled from Jeddah to paint the village, but without his paints he could only draw in grey. "Grey windows in Rijal Almaa!" he joked. "What a terrible idea."

That afternoon, Mr. Hassan finished his painting while Sami's family drank tea nearby. Before they said goodbye, he gave Sami a small extra picture he had painted quickly. It showed a boy holding a blue suitcase in front of the bright stone houses. Sami smiled, realising that the best part of his trip was the part nobody had planned.

pages.text: Yousef had never thought of archery as a real sport until the summer his grandfather took an old wooden bow down from the wall. "Your great-grandfather made this with his own hands," Grandpa Saleh said, running his fingers along the smooth wood. "He used to win every competition in the village." Yousef had only ever played football, but he couldn't help feeling curious.

Every evening after the heat had passed, they practised behind the farm, among the palm trees. Grandpa's eyes were weak now, so he could no longer shoot, but his ears were as sharp as ever. "Your feet are wrong," he would say, before Yousef had even let go of the arrow. At first, Yousef's arrows flew everywhere except the target, and his cousins teased him about it for weeks.

In October, his PE teacher told him about a youth archery competition in the city. Yousef signed up immediately, although he got butterflies in his stomach whenever he thought about it. The other archers would have expensive modern bows, while he only had a simple one made of wood. "A good archer doesn't depend on his bow," Grandpa said calmly. "He depends on his patience."

On the day of the competition, a strong wind was blowing across the field, and the flags were snapping loudly. Many archers were struggling, and their arrows kept landing at the edges of the target. Yousef's first arrows were not much better. By the final round, he was in fourth place, and he felt like giving up.

Then he noticed his grandfather sitting in the front row with his eyes closed. During the short break, Yousef walked over to him. "I can't see the wind, Grandpa," he said quietly. The old man smiled. "Neither can I. Stop trying to see it, and listen to the palm trees behind the field, the way I taught you."

Yousef returned to the line and took a deep breath. He closed his eyes for a moment and listened to the dry palm leaves rustling, louder and then softer. When the sound dropped, he opened his eyes, aimed slightly to the left, and released the arrow. It hit the yellow centre, and the crowd went silent before bursting into applause.

His last two arrows landed in the centre too, and Yousef jumped from fourth place to second. The winner, a tall boy called Hamad, came over to shake his hand. "I've never seen anyone shoot like that with a wooden bow," he said. "Who taught you?" Yousef proudly pointed to the old man in the front row.

That evening, the whole family gathered at Grandpa's house to celebrate with dates and Arabic coffee. Yousef hung his silver medal on the wall, right next to the old bow. "Next year it will be gold," his cousin joked. Yousef smiled. "Maybe," he said, "but today I learned something more valuable than gold: some things you can only see when you listen."

pages.text: Nobody on the farm liked the new robot at first, especially Grandpa Saleh. It arrived in a huge wooden box one burning morning in Al-Ahsa. It was tall and silver, with long arms for climbing date palms. 'A machine cannot understand trees,' Grandpa said, crossing his arms. 'You have to listen to a palm before you can look after it.' Faisal, who was thirteen and loved anything with a battery, secretly thought the robot was amazing.

The robot was called R-7, and it worked harder than ten people. It picked dates, checked the soil and repaired broken pipes without complaining. Every afternoon, Grandpa walked slowly between the trees, and R-7 followed him like a shadow. Grandpa never spoke to the robot, but he often talked to the palms about the old days. 'Once, a spring flowed here,' he would say quietly. 'It was the heart of this farm, but it dried up before your father was born.'

Then something strange started happening. Every morning, R-7's battery was almost empty, and its wheels were covered in wet mud. 'That's impossible,' said Faisal's older sister, Noura. 'It hasn't rained for months, and the robot is supposed to rest at night.' Faisal frowned. 'Maybe it's broken,' he said, although he didn't really believe it.

That night, the two of them climbed onto the roof and kept an eye on the robot's charging station. Just after midnight, R-7's lights flashed blue, and it rolled silently out of the gate. It didn't go towards the healthy trees. Instead, it headed for the forgotten corner of the farm, where only dry, dead palms stood in the sand.

Holding a torch, Faisal and Noura followed the tracks through the darkness. Soon they heard a scraping sound and saw R-7 bent over a circle of old stones. It was carefully removing sand and rocks with its long arms, as if it had been digging for weeks. On the small screen on its chest, three words were shining: TASK: HEART OF FARM.

'R-7, who gave you this job?' Noura asked. The robot turned its round head towards them, and a recording began to play in Grandpa's voice: 'It was the heart of this farm.' Faisal's mouth fell open. 'It's been listening to Grandpa all this time,' he whispered. Under the robot's wheels, the ground was dark and wet.

At sunrise, they brought Grandpa to the old stones, although he grumbled the whole way. He stopped suddenly when he heard it: the soft sound of water moving. A thin stream was running from the spring into the ancient channel, shining in the morning light. Grandpa knelt down and put his hand in the cool water, and his eyes filled with tears. 'I haven't seen this since I was a boy,' he said.

For a long moment, Grandpa looked at the robot that he had refused to trust. 'You listened better than any of us,' he finally said. 'From today, your name is Wafi, the faithful one.' Then he stood up, took the robot's metal hand and led it towards the oldest palm on the farm. 'Come,' he said with a smile. 'Now I will teach you how to hear a tree.'

options: Faisal told it about the spring.

options: He now trusts and respects it.

stories.title: The Letter in the Coral Wall

pages.text: The summer Omar turned fourteen, his family moved back into their old family house in Al-Balad, the historic heart of Jeddah. The house had been empty for nearly forty years, and builders were repairing its tall walls of coral stone. Omar thought it would be the most boring holiday of his life. Then one morning a builder called him over in a hurry. "Your sister has found something," the man said. "You'd better come and see."

Omar's older sister, Noura, was kneeling beside a hole where a stone had fallen out of the wall. Inside lay a small metal box, covered in rust and dust. "It must have been hidden here for a century," she whispered. Their father opened it carefully, and inside they found a folded letter, a brass key and an old photograph of a man standing proudly in front of the house.

The letter was written in beautiful Arabic handwriting, and their father read it aloud. "To my grandchildren's grandchildren," it began. "I built this house with my own hands in 1925, when ships from India and Egypt filled our harbour. If you are reading this, find what I have kept for you where the sea wind enters the house." Omar and Noura looked at each other, but neither of them had any idea what it meant.

For two days they searched every room, but they kept going round in circles. Then Grandmother, who had grown up in Al-Balad, gave them a clue over dinner. "In the old days, we didn't have air conditioners," she explained with a smile. "Every house had a mashrabiya, a wooden window that let the cool wind from the sea come inside." Noura jumped up so fast that she nearly knocked over her tea.

The biggest mashrabiya was on the top floor, and it faced west, towards the Red Sea. Under its wooden seat, Omar noticed a tiny lock that had been painted over many times. His hands were shaking as he tried the brass key, and for a moment nothing happened. Then, with a soft click, a narrow drawer slid open.

There was no gold inside, and at first Omar felt disappointed. Instead, there was a thick notebook full of drawings, prices and notes about the port: spices, cloth, coffee and the names of ships. Their great-great-grandfather had recorded everything he had seen at the harbour for over twenty years. "This isn't treasure," Omar said slowly. "It's even better. It's history that nobody has ever read."

Their father contacted a historian from the local museum, who came the very next day. She turned the pages with gloves on and could hardly believe her eyes. "Records like these are extremely rare," she told them. "They show us how ordinary people in Jeddah lived and worked a hundred years ago." She asked if the museum could make copies so that students across the Kingdom could learn from them.

Of course the family agreed, and the original notebook stayed safely in the house where it belonged. On the last night of the summer, Omar and Noura sat in the mashrabiya and wrote a letter of their own. They described their school, their hobbies and the city of glass towers that Jeddah had become. Then they placed it in the drawer, turned the key and smiled, because one day someone else would discover it.

pages.text: Every winter, Faisal's family drove south for a weekend by the sea, and this year they had come to the Farasan Islands. Their father had found a quiet beach far from the hotels, with soft white sand and water as clear as glass. Faisal and his younger sister, Reem, helped to put up the tent while the sun went down. "No phones tonight," their father said with a smile. "Tonight, we listen to the sea."

After dinner, their father hung a bright lamp from the tent pole and made tea on the small stove. Faisal was lying on a mat, staring up at more stars than he had ever seen in Riyadh. Suddenly, Reem sat up. "Something is moving in the sand," she whispered, pointing toward the dark beach.

At first, Faisal thought it was a crab. Then he saw another shape, and another, each one no bigger than his palm, pushing slowly across the sand on tiny flippers. "Baby turtles!" Reem gasped. But something was wrong, because the turtles were not crawling toward the sea. They were crawling straight toward the tent.

Faisal remembered a documentary he had watched at school. "Turtle hatchlings follow the brightest light," he explained. "Usually that's the moon shining on the water, but tonight it's our lamp!" Their father switched it off immediately, and the beach became completely dark. Without the lamp, however, the confused turtles stopped and turned in small circles, as if they had lost their way.

"Should we carry them to the water?" Reem asked. "No, our teacher said they need to walk there by themselves, so they'll remember this beach," Faisal replied. Reem looked up at the sky, where the moon was hiding behind a thick cloud. "Then let's build them a path," she said, "and wait for the moon to come back."

Working quietly, the children built two low walls of sand, like a narrow road leading from the tent down to the waves. Meanwhile, their father stood guard, chasing away the hungry crabs and seabirds. At last, the cloud moved away, and silver moonlight spread across the water. One by one, the hatchlings turned and began hurrying down the path while Faisal counted under his breath: twenty, forty, sixty...

By the time the sky turned pink, only one turtle was left, a tiny one with a damaged flipper that kept falling over. Reem knelt beside it, careful not to touch it. "Come on, little one, you can do it," she encouraged. A wave rushed up the beach, and when it slid back, the turtle was gone.

Later that morning, a ranger from the island's wildlife centre came to check the nest and listened to their story. He shook their father's hand and told the children that they had probably saved more than a hundred turtles. On the drive home, Reem asked, "Do you think that little turtle will ever come back to our beach?" Faisal grinned. "In about twenty years," he said, "and we'll be waiting for her, with the lights off."

pages.text: Lina had exactly three days to learn a dish she had never cooked. Her school in Riyadh was holding a cooking challenge to raise money for a local charity, and every team had to bring a traditional recipe from their family. "I'll make Grandma Noura's saleeg," she had announced confidently, although she had only ever eaten it. Now she was standing in the kitchen, staring at an old notebook full of strange drawings instead of words.

When Grandma Noura was young, she never had the chance to learn to read well, so she had invented her own way of writing recipes. A small cup meant rice, a cow meant milk, and three dots meant… nobody knew. "Why don't you just ask her?" said her brother Hamad, taking a date from the bowl. Lina sighed, because Grandma was visiting Aunt Huda in Abha, and her phone was always switched off.

On her first attempt, the rice stuck to the bottom of the pot and the whole flat smelled of smoke. On the second, it was so watery that Hamad asked if she was making soup. "I'm in hot water," Lina groaned, and Hamad laughed. "Literally," he said. That evening, their mother looked through the notebook and pointed at the last page, where Grandma had drawn a small clock next to a spoon.

"Your grandmother always stirred slowly and never rushed," her mother explained. "She used to say that saleeg can tell when you are impatient." Lina wasn't sure a pot of rice could feel anything, but the next morning she tried again. She turned the heat down low, stirred for forty minutes without checking her phone, and added the milk little by little. The rice became soft and creamy, but something was still missing.

Competition day arrived, and the school hall was filled with the smells of kabsa, mutabbaq and fresh bread. Lina's best friend and teammate, Reem, tasted the saleeg and frowned slightly. "It's good," she said kindly, "but it doesn't taste like your grandma's." Lina's heart sank, because the judges would arrive in less than an hour.

Then her phone buzzed with a message from an unknown number. It was Grandma, who had borrowed Aunt Huda's phone after hearing about the challenge. Lina quickly sent a photo of the three mysterious dots, and a voice message came back almost immediately. "Habibti, those are cardamom seeds!" Grandma laughed. "Crush them and add them at the end, with a little ghee on top."

Reem ran to the teachers' room, where she remembered seeing a jar of cardamom next to the coffee pot. Lina crushed the seeds with the back of a spoon, stirred them in, and finished the dish with a spoonful of melted ghee. A warm, sweet smell rose from the pot, and suddenly she felt six years old again, sitting in Grandma's kitchen. The judges arrived just as she placed the last bowl on the table.

Lina's team didn't win first prize; that went to a boy whose kleija looked as if it had come from a bakery. However, the judges gave them a special award for "Best Family Story" after Lina explained the picture notebook. That weekend, when Grandma came home, Lina cooked saleeg for the whole family without opening the notebook once. "Now you know the secret," Grandma said with a smile as she tasted it. "Patience, a little cardamom, and someone to cook for."

options: She never had the chance to learn to read well when she was young

options: Three spoons of sugar

options: The water in her pot is too hot

options: She should cook the saleeg very quickly

options: Cooking for people you love is part of what makes food special

pages.text: It was the first week of the summer holidays, and Faisal's mother had asked him to help clear out the dusty storeroom on the roof. Behind a pile of old carpets, he noticed a strange wooden case covered in dust. When he opened it, he found an oud with a long crack across its body and two strings missing. He carried it downstairs carefully, as if it were made of glass.

"Where did you find that?" his grandfather asked, and his eyes suddenly looked younger. He explained that he had played this oud at family weddings in Taif for nearly forty years. "Then my hands began to shake, and I couldn't play properly anymore," he said quietly. "So I put it away, because it hurt too much to look at it." Faisal had never known that his grandfather was a musician.

The next morning, Faisal took the oud to Uncle Hamza, an old instrument maker who had a tiny shop in the souq. Uncle Hamza turned it over slowly and whistled. "This is excellent wood, but repairing it won't be cheap or quick," he warned. Faisal emptied his savings box onto the counter, money he had been keeping for a new phone, and said, "Please, I'll wait as long as it takes."

Three weeks later, the oud was as good as new, and Grandfather became Faisal's teacher. Although he couldn't play himself, he hummed each melody and told Faisal exactly where to put his fingers. At first, Faisal's fingertips were so sore that he wanted to give up. "Pain is the price of every beautiful sound," his grandfather said with a smile, so Faisal kept practising every evening after dinner.

In September, the school announced a Heritage Evening, and students were invited to share something from Saudi culture. Faisal signed up before he could change his mind. His cousin Nawaf laughed and said, "An oud? Nobody our age is interested in that old-fashioned stuff." That night, Faisal couldn't sleep because he had butterflies in his stomach, but he decided he wouldn't let Nawaf's words stop him.

On the evening of the show, the hall was full of parents, teachers and students, and Grandfather was sitting in the front row. Faisal walked onto the stage, sat down and began the old Taif melody his grandfather loved. Everything was going perfectly until, halfway through the song, there was a sharp sound. One of the strings had broken, and the hall went completely silent.

Faisal's face burned, and for a moment he wanted to run off the stage. Then he looked down at the front row, where his grandfather had started clapping a slow, steady rhythm. Soon the parents around him joined in, and then the whole hall was clapping together. Taking a deep breath, Faisal found new places for his fingers and continued the melody on just five strings.

When the last note faded, the audience jumped to their feet and cheered, and even Nawaf was clapping the loudest. Afterwards, Grandfather held Faisal's hands in his own shaking ones. "Tonight you didn't just play music," he said. "You gave my oud its voice back, and you gave me mine too." Faisal realised that some things are worth far more than a new phone.

options: Faisal had taught him to sing

stories.title: The Watch That Should Not Tick

pages.text: Faris spent every Saturday at his grandfather's watch shop in the old part of Jeddah. The shop was small and dusty and full of ticking clocks, and he loved it more than any shopping mall. In the window sat Grandfather's most precious possession: a silver pocket watch that had belonged to his own grandfather. Its hands always pointed to quarter to four, because nobody had wound it for sixty years. "Some things are more beautiful when they rest," Grandfather liked to say.

That Saturday, a well-dressed man in a grey thobe came in and asked to see the silver watch. He held it for a long time, turning it over in his hands and taking photos of it with his phone. "I'll pay you twenty thousand riyals for it," he offered. Grandfather smiled politely and shook his head. "I'm sorry, but it isn't for sale at any price."

The next morning, Faris arrived early to help Yousef, the young apprentice, open the shop. As he walked past the window, he stopped suddenly. The silver watch looked exactly the same as always, but something felt wrong. He bent closer and heard a soft, steady sound: tick, tick, tick.

"Grandfather, your watch is working!" Faris called. Grandfather hurried over, picked it up and frowned. "This isn't my watch," he said quietly. "It's a very good copy, but whoever made it forgot one important detail." Yousef went pale, because he was the only other person with a key to the shop.

Grandfather looked worried, but Faris refused to believe that Yousef was guilty. He remembered the man in the grey thobe and all the photos he had taken. "Someone needed those photos to make a copy," he said slowly. "But they still had to get close enough to swap the watches." He looked around the shop carefully, just like the detectives in his favourite books.

Faris asked Yousef whether anyone had come in after Grandfather left for the Maghrib prayer the evening before. Yousef thought for a moment. "The man in the grey thobe came back," he admitted. "He wanted one last look at the watch, so I gave it to him while I answered the phone." Faris and Grandfather looked at each other, then up at the small camera above the door.

On the video, they watched the man take something from his pocket and swap the two watches in less than three seconds. Grandfather phoned the police straight away, and they found the man before the end of the day. He had been planning to sell the real watch to a collector abroad. By evening, the silver watch was back in Grandfather's hands, still showing quarter to four.

That night, Yousef apologised again and again for his mistake. "You were tricked by a clever thief," Grandfather said kindly. "The important thing is that you told the truth." Then he turned to Faris with a proud smile. "A clock that ticks can be useful, but a detective who listens is priceless."

questions.q: Why did the silver watch always show quarter to four?
options: Because nobody had wound it for sixty years

options: It was a different colour

options: A rich customer

options: He was afraid people would think he stole it

options: Faris should become a watchmaker

pages.text: Yousef discovered his strange power on the most boring afternoon of his life. He was sitting at the back of the classroom while his teacher talked about rocks, and nobody was looking at him. Suddenly, he glanced down and saw that his hands had disappeared. He could still feel his fingers, but he couldn't see them at all.

After a week of secret experiments in his bedroom, Yousef understood the rules. He became invisible only when nobody in the world was thinking about him. The moment someone remembered him, like his mother calling him for dinner or his little sister Noura looking for her charger, he appeared again. "It's not exactly a superpower," he complained to his grandfather, the only person he had told. "It's a superpower for people nobody notices."

Grandfather put down his cup of tea and smiled. "Every power has a purpose, Yousef. Perhaps yours is waiting for the right moment." Yousef wasn't convinced. Heroes in films could fly or lift cars, but he could only vanish when he felt forgotten.

The right moment came on a busy Thursday evening at a shopping mall in Jeddah. Yousef's family was buying shoes when the lights went out and an alarm began to scream. Smoke was pouring from a kitchen near the food court, and hundreds of people rushed towards the exits in panic. In the confusion, Yousef heard a small voice crying behind a storeroom door.

A security guard was shouting into his radio, and nobody was paying attention to a quiet fourteen-year-old. Yousef felt the familiar tingle and watched his body fade into nothing. He slipped through a gap in a barrier that the guards would never have let him pass. Inside the storeroom, a boy of about six was hiding under a shelf, coughing and terrified.

"I can't see you!" the boy whispered when Yousef spoke to him. "That's fine. Just hold my hand and keep your head down," Yousef said calmly, although his own heart was racing. Together they crawled along the floor, where the air was cleaner, until they reached an emergency exit that was blocked by boxes. Yousef pushed the boxes aside one by one and led the boy out into the cool night air.

The boy's father ran forward and hugged his son, looking around in surprise for the person who had helped him. Then Yousef heard his mother's voice calling his name desperately. At that moment his whole family was thinking about him, and he reappeared, covered in dust. His mother held him tightly, Noura burst into tears, and his father kept saying "Alhamdulillah" again and again.

Later that night, Grandfather sat beside Yousef on the balcony. "So, is it still a useless power?" he asked with a twinkle in his eye. Yousef laughed and shook his head. He had learned something important that evening. Being invisible had helped him save someone, but becoming visible again because people loved him felt even better.

questions.q: When does Yousef become invisible?
options: When nobody is thinking about him
When he closes his eyes
When he feels very angry

questions.q: Who was the only person Yousef told about his power at first?
options: His sister Noura

pages.text: Faris had been counting the days until the camping trip to the Nafud desert. On Thursday afternoon, his father and Uncle Saad loaded the car with a tent, blankets, a gas cooker and enough water for three days. His cousin Nawaf, who was only eleven, had brought something special: a small drone with a camera. "I'm going to film the best sunset in Saudi Arabia," he announced proudly.

By the time they had set up the tent among the red dunes, the sun was already low. Father lit a fire and made cardamom coffee while Uncle Saad cooked chicken kabsa in a big pot. Nawaf sent his drone high into the golden sky, and the boys watched the screen in amazement. Then a strong wind suddenly blew from the north, and the drone disappeared behind a tall dune.

"My birthday present!" Nawaf cried. "Don't worry, it can't be far," Faris said. Without telling the adults, the two boys ran after the signal on the controller. They climbed one dune, then another, and soon they had completely lost track of time.

They finally found the drone lying in the soft sand, its battery almost empty. Faris turned around to lead the way back, but his heart sank. Every dune looked exactly the same in the fading light, and the wind had already erased their footprints. Even worse, his phone had no signal, and Nawaf's controller had just died.

Nawaf's voice began to shake. "We're lost, aren't we?" Faris felt afraid too, but he knew that panicking would only make things worse. He closed his eyes and remembered his grandfather's words on the roof of their house in Hail: "When the sand lies to you, the sky will tell you the truth."

As darkness covered the desert, the stars appeared one by one. Faris searched the sky until he found the seven bright stars his grandfather called Banat Na'sh, and they led his eyes to a small, steady star: Al-Jadi, the North Star. "The wind came from the north, so it blew the drone south," he explained. "That means our camp is north of us. We just have to walk towards that star."

They walked slowly, holding hands and keeping the star in front of them. After about twenty minutes, Nawaf pointed and shouted. Far away, a small orange light was flickering at the bottom of a dune: the campfire! They could also hear Uncle Saad's voice calling their names across the sand.

Father hugged them both tightly, then gave them a long, serious look. "You should never have left without telling us," he said, "but I'm proud that you kept a cool head." Later that night, Faris called his grandfather, who laughed warmly when he heard the whole story. "The sky has guided our people for a thousand years," the old man said, "and now it's your turn to teach Nawaf."

pages.text: Every Monday, Yousef stayed after the last bell to empty the school's lost-and-found box. Most weeks it held the usual things: odd socks from PE, a broken ruler, someone's forgotten water bottle. But this Monday, under a pile of jackets, he found something he had never seen before. It was a small notebook with a faded blue cover and no name on it.

He opened it, expecting someone's maths homework. Instead, every page was covered with pencil drawings of the school: the main gate, the science lab, the old palm tree by the car park. They were so detailed that Yousef could almost hear the noise of the playground. "Whoever drew these is seriously talented," he whispered.

The next morning he showed the notebook to his best friend, Hamad. "Just put a notice on the board," Hamad suggested. "The owner will come for it." But three days passed, and nobody came. "Finding the artist in a school of six hundred students is like looking for a needle in a haystack," Hamad sighed.

Yousef refused to give up. That evening he studied the drawings more carefully and noticed something strange. In one picture, the library had a wooden door, but that door had been replaced with a glass one years ago. In another, the palm tree was only as tall as a man, although now it reached the roof.

"These weren't drawn recently," Yousef told Hamad at break. "Some of them must be twenty or thirty years old." Hamad's eyes widened. "So the owner isn't a student at all?" Together they made a list of everyone who had worked at the school for a long time, and only one name had been there longer than the palm tree: Uncle Saleh, the caretaker.

They found him in the small workshop behind the gym, fixing a broken chair. When Yousef held up the notebook, the old man's face lit up. "I thought I'd lost this forever!" he exclaimed. He explained that he had drawn the school every year since he arrived, and that he was retiring at the end of the month. "I wanted to take my memories with me," he said quietly.

Walking home, Yousef couldn't stop thinking about what he had heard. Uncle Saleh had looked after the school for thirty-two years, yet most students didn't even know his name. "We should do something for him," he told Hamad, who grinned and agreed immediately. With the headteacher's permission, they spent two weeks secretly scanning the drawings and preparing a surprise.

On Uncle Saleh's last day, he was asked to come to the school hall. When the doors opened, he saw his drawings printed in large frames along the walls, and hundreds of students clapping. Beside each picture, a student had written a thank-you note. The old man wiped his eyes and turned to Yousef. "You returned more than a notebook, my son," he said. "You gave me back thirty-two years."

pages.text: Lina had always thought her grandmother's storeroom was full of nothing but dust and old carpets. But that Friday afternoon, the family was preparing for Grandma Noura to move into their house in Jeddah, and Lina found a small wooden box hidden behind a pile of blankets. Inside was a cassette tape with faded handwriting on the label: "For Noura – 1979." Lina's heart began to beat faster.

"That's Grandpa's writing," said her older brother, Omar, looking over her shoulder. Their grandfather had died before Lina was born, and she knew him only from photographs and the stories her father told at dinner. "We have to play it," she whispered. The problem was that nobody in the family had owned a cassette player for at least twenty years.

After searching the whole house, they finally discovered an ancient player in a cupboard in their father's study. Omar pressed the button, but nothing happened except a sad clicking sound. "It's broken," he sighed. "Maybe we should just forget about it." Lina refused to give up so easily, and she remembered a tiny electronics shop in Al-Balad, the old part of the city, where her father used to get his watch repaired.

The next evening, their father drove them through the narrow streets, past the tall coral-stone houses with their wooden balconies. The shop owner, an elderly man called Abu Saleh, examined the machine through thick glasses. "The belt inside has worn out," he explained, "but I think I still have one somewhere." While he worked, he told them that people used to send recorded messages to their families when phone calls abroad were too expensive.

When they got home, Lina and Omar shut themselves in her bedroom and pressed play. At first there was only a soft hiss, and then a young man's voice filled the room, warm and slightly nervous. "Assalamu alaikum, Noura. It's snowing here in Colorado, and I have never been so cold in my life!" Lina and Omar stared at each other in amazement, because the voice sounded almost exactly like their father's.

On the tape, Grandpa described his engineering classes, his kind neighbours and his terrible first attempt at cooking kabsa alone. He laughed at himself so much that Omar couldn't stop laughing too. Near the end, his voice became quieter. "I've started writing a poem for you, but I'll only finish it when I'm home again," he said, and he recited the first lines. Then the tape suddenly stopped.

"He never finished it," Lina said sadly. Omar frowned. "Or maybe he did, but not on tape." They decided to keep their secret until Grandma Noura had settled into her new room. On her first evening with them, after the family had eaten dinner together, Lina placed the old player on the table and asked everyone to listen.

As soon as she heard the voice, Grandma Noura put her hand over her mouth, and her eyes filled with tears. Their father sat completely still, as if he were listening to a stranger he had always known. When the tape reached the unfinished poem, Grandma closed her eyes and, in a soft, steady voice, recited the final lines that Grandpa had written for her more than forty years ago. Nobody spoke for a long moment, and then Grandma smiled at Lina and said, "Thank you for bringing him home."

pages.text: Faisal's grandfather, Abu Saleh, had grown dates in Al-Ahsa for fifty years, and he didn't trust anything with a screen. "A palm tree speaks to the man who listens," he liked to say. So when Faisal arrived for the summer holidays with a box of tiny sensors and a tablet, his grandfather raised an eyebrow. "What are those? Toys?"

"They're soil sensors, Grandpa," Faisal explained. "If the ground gets too dry, they send a message to my phone." He had built them himself for a school science competition, using a cheap kit and a lot of online videos. His grandfather laughed kindly, but he agreed to let Faisal put them under five of the oldest palms.

For the first week, nothing interesting happened. Every morning, the screen showed five green circles, which meant the soil was healthy. Faisal's cousin Noura, who was visiting with her family, teased him about it. "Your invention is very good at saying 'everything is fine'," she said with a grin.

Then, at three o'clock one night, Faisal's phone buzzed loudly. One circle had turned red: Tree 4 – soil dry. He frowned, confused, because the water pump had been running for hours. Something didn't add up, so he grabbed a torch and went to wake his grandfather.

At first, Abu Saleh was annoyed, but he got up anyway. Out on the dark farm, the air was hot and heavy, and they could hear the pump humming steadily. Faisal pointed his torch at Tree 4. The ground around it was cracked and dusty, even though water should have been flowing there.

His grandfather knelt down and pressed his hand against the earth, then walked slowly along the line of the old pipe. About twenty metres away, he stopped. "Listen," he whispered. Under the sand, they heard a faint sound of rushing water – the pipe had broken, and the water was disappearing deep underground instead of reaching the trees.

By sunrise, they had dug up the broken piece and replaced it with help from Faisal's uncle. "In this heat, the trees would have suffered for days before I noticed," Abu Saleh admitted, wiping his forehead. "Your little machine heard the problem, but it took an old man's ears to find it." Faisal smiled, because he realised they had both been right.

Before the holiday ended, his grandfather asked for ten more sensors – one for every row of palms. He even gave Tree 4 a nickname: "the Messenger". Back at school, Faisal won second prize in the competition, but his favourite moment wasn't on the stage. It was a voice message from Grandpa that said, "Green circles today. The Messenger says hello."
